'''George Elwood Smith''' (May 10, 1930 – May 28, 2025) was an American applied [[physicist]] and a co-inventor of the [[charge-coupled device]] (CCD). Smith shared one half of the 2009 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] with [[Willard Boyle]] "for the invention of an imaging semiconductor circuit - the CCD sensor."<ref name="Nobel Prize">{{Cite web|title=Nobel Prize in Physics 2009 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2009/summary/|url-status=live |publisher=NobelPrize.org|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091008215314/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2009/index.html|archive-date=2009-10-08|access-date=2009-10-06}}</ref>

== Education ==
George Elwood Smith was born on May 10, 1930, in [[White Plains, New York]]. After serving in the [[United States Navy]] for four years and taking courses at the [[University of Miami]], Smith qualified in 1952 as a sophomore at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], where he majored in physics and graduated with honors in 1955. He then became a graduate student of the [[University of Chicago]], where he also worked as a teaching assistant.<ref name="Nobel bio">{{Cite web |title=George E. Smith – Biographical |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2009/smith/biographical/|url-status=live |publisher=NobelPrize.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251111202439/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2009/smith/biographical/|archive-date=2025-11-11|access-date=2026-02-09}}</ref> He received a [[Master of Science]] in 1956 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (Ph.D.) in 1959.<ref name="AIP">{{Cite web|title=Smith, George E., 1930-|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11506006.html|url-status=dead|publisher=American Institute of Physics|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241203184036/https://history.aip.org/phn/11506006.html
|archive-date=2024-12-03|access-date=2026-05-14}}</ref> At the time, his eight-page thesis on the electronic properties of [[semimetal]]s was the shortest Ph.D. thesis in the history of the university.<ref name="Nokia">{{Cite web|last1=Klein|first1=Thierry E.|last2=Vetter|first2=Peter|date=June 9, 2025 |title=In Memoriam – George E. Smith, Co-Inventor of the Charge-Coupled Device |url=https://www.nokia.com/blog/in-memoriam-george-e-smith-co-inventor-of-the-charge-coupled-device/|publisher=Nokia|access-date=November 1, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Smith |first=George E.|year=1959|title=The Anomalous Skin Effect in Bismuth|degree=Ph.D. |bibcode=1959PhRv..115.1561S|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.115.1561|id={{ProQuest|301893432}}}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1959, Smith joined the Technical Staff of [[Bell Telephone Laboratories]] in [[Murray Hill, New Jersey]], where he headed the Device Concepts Group from 1964 until his retirement in 1986.<ref name="AIP"/> His work was done in the [[Very-large-scale integration|VLSI]] Device Department at Bell Labs.<ref name="Nobel bio"/>

In 1969, Smith and [[Willard Boyle]], a fellow Bell Labs researcher, invented the [[charge-coupled device]], for which they were awarded the 2009 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]].

== Personal life and death ==
In 1955, Smith married his wife Janet, with whom he had three children. They often sailed on weekends until her death in 1975.<ref name="Nobel bio"/><ref name="Nokia"/>

After retirement, Smith and his life partner sailed around the world for seventeen years, crossing the [[Atlantic Ocean]] twice and sailing through the [[Panama Canal]]. They returned to New Jersey in 2003.<ref name="Nokia"/> He resided in the [[Waretown, New Jersey|Waretown]] section of [[Ocean Township, Ocean County, New Jersey]].<ref>Staff. [https://6abc.com/archive/7050733/ "NJ man's discovery lands Nobel Prize"], [[WPVI-TV]], October 6, 2009. Accessed November 27, 2013. "George E. Smith, 79, holds a display with a photograph of the first video telephone and some early CCD chips at his home in Waretown, N.J., Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2009, after it was announced that he had won the Nobel Prize in physics."</ref>

Smith died at his home in [[Barnegat Township, New Jersey]], on May 28, 2025, at the age of 95.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Loeb McClain|first=Dylan|date=2025-05-30|title=George E. Smith, Nobel Winner Who Created a Digital Eye, Dies at 95|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/30/science/george-e-smith-dead.html|url-access=subscription|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2025-05-30}}</ref>
